title: In Search of Excellence
author: Thomas J. Peters and Robert H. Waterman Jr.
theme: Excellent companies win less through clever analysis than through a handful of practical, people-centred habits that keep them close to action, customers and shared values.
summary: Tom Peters and Robert Waterman were consultants at McKinsey when they set out to answer a simple question: what do well-run American companies have in common? At a time when many believed Japanese firms had overtaken the United States, they studied a group of large companies with long records of growth, innovation and financial success, and looked for patterns in how they actually behaved.

Their main argument is that management had become too rational. Business schools and planners treated organisations as machines to be optimised with numbers, strategy charts and structure. The excellent companies, by contrast, paid close attention to people, values and the informal side of the organisation, and treated analysis as a servant rather than a master.

The authors describe eight shared attributes. The firms had a bias for action, preferring quick experiments to endless study. They stayed close to the customer, learning from the people they served and obsessing over quality and service. They encouraged autonomy and entrepreneurship, letting small teams act like independent ventures and tolerating failure. They sought productivity through people, treating employees as the main source of improvement rather than as costs.

They were hands-on and value-driven, with leaders who visibly lived a few clear beliefs. They stuck to the knitting, staying near the businesses they knew best rather than diversifying widely. They kept a simple form and lean staff, avoiding complex structures and large headquarters. Finally, they combined loose and tight properties: firm control over a few core values, with wide freedom for people to act within them.

The book became one of the best-selling business books ever, though later critics noted that several of the featured companies stumbled within a few years. Its lasting contribution is the reminder that culture, customers and people are central to performance.
takeaway: Act quickly, stay close to customers, trust people, keep structures simple, and hold firmly to a few core values while giving freedom on the rest.

questions.q: What was the central question behind the authors' research?
options: Why do start-ups fail in their first year?
What common practices do consistently successful large companies share?
How should companies expand into Japan?
Which financial ratios best predict share prices?
questions.why: Peters and Waterman studied high-performing companies to find the shared behaviours behind their long-run success.

questions.q: What did the authors criticise in the management thinking of their time?
options: Too much attention to employee welfare
Too little use of computers
An over-reliance on rational, numbers-driven analysis
Excessive focus on customer service
questions.why: They argued that a narrow rational model ignored people, values and culture, which mattered greatly in excellent firms.

questions.q: A 'bias for action' means a company tends to:
options: Try things quickly and learn by experimenting
Delay decisions until all data is collected
Reward only the most senior managers
Copy competitors' products
questions.why: Excellent firms preferred fast, practical experiments over long cycles of study and committee review.

questions.q: What does 'stick to the knitting' recommend?
options: Diversify into as many industries as possible
Focus only on cost cutting
Outsource core activities
Stay close to the businesses the company knows best
questions.why: The authors found that the best performers rarely strayed far from their core skills and markets.

questions.q: How did the excellent companies view their employees?
options: As a cost to be minimised
As the main source of quality and productivity gains
As interchangeable parts
As less important than equipment
questions.why: 'Productivity through people' meant treating employees with respect and as the root of improvement.

questions.q: Which attribute describes firm control over a few core values combined with wide freedom elsewhere?
options: Simple form, lean staff
Close to the customer
Simultaneous loose-tight properties
Hands-on, value-driven
questions.why: Loose-tight properties mean being strict about central values while decentralising day-to-day decisions.

questions.q: What did 'autonomy and entrepreneurship' look like in practice?
options: Small teams encouraged to act like independent ventures and allowed to fail
Every decision approved by headquarters
Banning internal competition
Rewarding only flawless results
questions.why: The firms fostered internal champions and small units, accepting that some experiments would fail.

questions.q: What kind of organisational structure did the excellent companies tend to have?
options: Complex matrix structures with many reporting lines
Large corporate headquarters staffs
Frequent major reorganisations
Simple structures with lean central staff
questions.why: 'Simple form, lean staff' captures their preference for clarity and few layers at the top.

options: Leaders who visibly practise a few clear beliefs and stay in touch with the work
Managers who avoid the shop floor
Setting values by consultants only
Running the firm purely by budgets
questions.why: Leaders in excellent firms shaped culture by living core values and staying close to operations.

questions.q: What criticism did the book face in later years?
options: It ignored the role of customers
Several of the featured companies ran into difficulties soon after publication
It was written only for small businesses
It recommended heavy diversification
questions.why: Critics pointed out that some 'excellent' firms stumbled, questioning whether the attributes guaranteed lasting success.
